newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Visa card volume up 24 pct in year.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Visa card volume up 24 pct in year.

text.p: Rapid Growth outside of the U.S. has helped push Visa card volume to record levels, Visa International president and chief executive Edmund Jensen said Monday.
While various reward programs have driven growth in the U.S., Jensen said, "in the rest of the world people are discovering that they would rather use a payment card than cash."
Jensen spoke by telephone from the San Francisco headquarters of Visa, an association made up of banks and other organizations which issue cards.

Purchases of goods and services with Visa cards rose 23.7 percent to a record $1 trillion in the 12 months ended March 31, Visa said. The association said it is the first card group in the world to reach $1 trillion in transaction volume in a 12-month period. In the 12 months ending March 31, 1996, volume totaled $824 billion.

Jensen noted that spending on Visa cards, which includes corporate cards used by businesses, has doubled in the last three years. "We expect we will continue to double, and be twice the size three years from now," he said.
In much of the world, Jensen said, the Visa cards are debit cards, which involve a deduction from a deposit account rather than accumulation of a credit balance.
In the 12 months ended March 31, worldwide transactions on Visa debit cards rose 40 percent to a record $305 billion.

Some of the countries where use of payment cards is growing rapidly, although from a small base, include China, Brazil and Hungary. Russia also proved fertile ground for payment cards. "There is a huge thirst in Russia," Jensen said. However, he said, due to a lack of financial infrastructure, the product had to be tailored to the market.

In Hungary, Jensen said, Visa cards have grown from zero to 500,000 in a short time. In China, there are 12 million Visa cards in use compared to about one million three years ago. The total is expected to reach 20 million next year.
Jensen said the 24 percent year-over-year growth rate is creating a vast pool of consumers who will be able to use the Internet for commerce.

Jensen said that in addition to the convenience that cards offer, another driver for the growing use of cards is the desire of governments in emerging markets to move from an underground economy to a payment system that creates records and therefore can be used to collect taxes.

Jensen said while Visa transactions are growing rapidly, the penetration of the total payments market including checks and cash is still small. Although the number of transactions with checks is still rising, the growth rate has fallen. Jensen predicted that sooner or later the number of check transactions will fall.
He said Visa accounts for just over five percent of global personal expenditures. But the low penetration means that there is a huge growth potential, he added.
As of March 31, there were 572 million Visa cards worldwide, up 12.8 percent from a year earlier.
